The Git History view shows the commit history, 15 revision graph, commit details, and affected resources for the selected repository, branch, or 16 resource. The view opens at the bottom of the application interface. You can open it in any of 17 the following ways:

18

36
Main Areas

The main areas in the Git History 38 view are:

    39
  • Repository and branch header - Shows 40 the repository name and the current branch.
    • 41
  • Toolbar and text filter - Controls the history 44 view.
    • 45
  • History table - Shows the revision graph, commit 48 messages, dates, authors, commit IDs, and uncommitted changes.
    • 49
  • Commit details pane - Shows details for the selected 52 commit.
    • 53
  • Affected resources pane - Lists the files changed by 56 the selected commit.

58
Toolbar and Filter

Use the toolbar to control which commits are shown in the 60 history table.

    61
  • Branch Chooser - Choose 62 All branches, All local branches, 63 Current branch, or Current local 64 branch.
    • 65
  • Link 67 with Editor - Synchronizes the history with the selected editor. It is 68 enabled by default.
    • 69
  • Refresh - Reloads the displayed 71 history.
    • 72
  • Text Filter - Filters the history 73 by commit message, date, author, commit ID, branch name, or tag name.
    • 74
75
History Table

The history table shows commits in rows. The graph column 77 shows how commits are connected, and the other columns show the commit message, date, 78 author, and commit ID.

For each commit in 79 the history table, the following context menu actions are available:

Select more than one commit to compare the changes 149 across a range of revisions. The lower panes show the boundary commits and the files changed 150 in the selected range.

151 Git History Range Comparison 152 154

When you select two or more 155 committed revisions, the lower panes compare the newest and oldest selected commits. The 156 left pane identifies the compared revisions, while the right pane lists all files changed 157 between those two endpoints.

158

The contextual actions in the changed-files 159 list depend on the change type:

160
    161
  • Modified and 162 renamed files provide actions to compare the newer version with 163 the older version and to open the newer, older, or working-copy version when 164 available.
    • 165
  • Added files provide actions to 166 open the newer version and, when the file still exists locally, the working-copy 167 version.
    • 168
  • Deleted files provide an action 169 to open the older version.

When a merge, rebase, cherry-pick, or revert is in 172 progress, the history view highlights the commits involved by adding amber labels to the 173 corresponding commits in the graph. These labels help you identify the incoming commit, the 174 reverted or cherry-picked commit, or the start point of the current operation. For more 175 information, see .

176

The history table can also show an 177 Uncommitted changes row. Select it to inspect the working-copy 178 changes that are not committed yet.

179

180 181 Git History Uncommitted Changes 182 184 185

186

If you select the Uncommitted 187 changes row together with one or more committed revisions, the lower panes 188 compare the current working tree with the oldest selected revision. The left pane identifies 189 the working tree and the selected revision, while the right pane lists all files that differ 190 between them.

191

In this working-tree comparison mode, modified and 192 renamed files can be compared directly with the selected revision, added files can be opened 193 from the working copy, and deleted files can be opened at the selected revision.

194

When a range comparison produces no differences, the 195 changed-files pane shows a No changes. message. When the 196 Uncommitted changes row is selected by itself and there are no 197 unstaged changes, the pane shows No unstaged changes..

File conflicts happen when users modify the same file 7 in 8 different branches and then try to apply one branch's changes onto the 9 other. File conflicts can occur during a merge or merge-like operation such as a rebase, 10 cherry-pick, or revert.

11

To resolve a file conflict, on Git Staging, follow these steps:

12

13

    14
  1. Open the file in the 15 compare 16 editor to view the differences between the local and incoming version. 17

    To do so, 18 on 19 Unstaged files, double-click the conflicted file. 22 Alternatively, right-click the file to open the context menu and choose Open 23 in compare editor.

    24 25 A conflicted file's context menu 26 28 29

    2. 30
  2. Choose how to resolve the conflict.
      31
    1. If both versions modify the same file and you want to keep changes from both 32 versions; on the compare editor, choose which changes to keep and discard. To resolve 33 the conflict, select Apply.
      2. 34
    2. If both versions modify the same file and one version is the clear choice, use Resolve using Mine to keep the working copy version 37 or Resolve using Theirs to accept the incoming 40 version.

      To do so, right-click a conflicted resource to open the context menu and 41 choose Resolve using "Mine" or Resolve using 42 "Theirs".

      3. 43
    3. To mark a file conflict as resolved (even if it is not), right-click a conflicted 44 resource and select Mark as resolved.
      4. 47
    3. 48
